title: Song Offerings to the World
subtitle: How a poet’s village songs crossed oceans and returned as a school under the sky
moral: A voice rooted at home can still speak to the world.

sources.citation: Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (Bengali, 1910) and Gitanjali: Song Offerings (London, 1912)
sources.note: Primary Bengali collection and English creative reworking.

sources.citation: Nobel Prize in Literature citation for Rabindranath Tagore, November 13, 1913
Tagore's letter returning his knighthood, May 30, 1919
sources.note: Primary protest after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

sources.citation: Oxford Tagore Translations project (Oxford University Press, 2010-) and scholarship on the English Gitanjali
sources.note: Recent translation work showing differences between Bengali originals and English versions.

panels.shot: epic medium-wide of Tagore seated under a banyan in Santiniketan, manuscripts in hand, faint silhouettes of ships and a snowy European cityscape rising behind him like clouds

dialogue.text: From songs born in a quiet Bengal courtyard to the Nobel in distant Stockholm, how did Rabindranath Tagore turn world fame into a school beneath the open sky?

panels.shot: intimate interior wide of Jorasanko mansion, lamplit, with Tagore at a desk surrounded by Bengali manuscripts

dialogue.text: Calcutta, 1910. In the Jorasanko house, Rabindranath gathers years of verse into a single Bengali volume he calls Gitanjali, song-offerings for an unseen listener.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Tagore’s hand writing with a pen, Bengali lines on one side, English prose on another notebook

dialogue.text: Two years later, on the voyage to England and in quiet stops, he reshapes these songs into English prose, not line by line, but as fresh offerings in another tongue.

panels.shot: medium shot in a small London drawing room, Tagore reading softly as a small mixed group of British listeners lean forward

dialogue.text: In London parlours, he reads these prose songs aloud. The English is simple, almost bare, yet in the still rooms, listeners hear something new and very old at once.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of a British poet (un-cast silhouette) holding the Gitanjali manuscript with scribbled preface notes, Tagore in soft focus beyond

dialogue.text: Friends and poets in England carry his manuscript to a publisher. Their prefaces and praise open doors his own quiet voice might not have reached alone.

panels.shot: graphic close-up of the title page of Gitanjali: Song Offerings being opened by Tagore, his face reflected faintly in the glass of a window

dialogue.text: In 1912, Gitanjali: Song Offerings appears in London, one hundred and three pieces of prose, drawn from the Bengali volume yet altered, pruned, merged, as if rewritten for another ear.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye of a map from Calcutta to London to Stockholm, with Tagore’s small figure walking along an ink-drawn line

dialogue.text: The prose poems travel further than he does. In Stockholm, academicians read them in English and translation, arguing over their strangeness and their clarity.

panels.shot: medium-wide of Tagore in Santiniketan receiving a telegram, students and trees around him

dialogue.text: On 13 November 1913, a telegram reaches Santiniketan. Rabindranath Tagore is named the first non-European Nobel laureate in Literature, honoured for his deeply sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse.

panels.shot: close-up on Tagore’s face as he reads the telegram, a mix of surprise and inwardness

dialogue.speaker: rabindranath_tagore
dialogue.text: This honour belongs first to the songs, and to the land that shaped them.

panels.shot: formal medium shot of Tagore at a modest ceremony in India, being addressed as Nobel laureate, British officials present

dialogue.text: In cities and courts he is celebrated, knighted by the British Crown soon after. Yet he returns again and again to Santiniketan, seeing the Nobel not as an arrival, but as a resource.

panels.shot: wide pastoral shot of Santiniketan classes under trees, Tagore walking among children

dialogue.text: He pours royalties and gifts into this experiment in learning under the sky, shaping Santiniketan into Visva-Bharati, a world-university rooted in village soil.

panels.shot: medium shot of Tagore speaking with a small group of Indian and foreign teachers under a verandah

dialogue.speaker: rabindranath_tagore
dialogue.text: Let the cultures of the world meet here, without walls between child and earth.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Tagore alone at a desk at night, newspapers about world war and nationalism scattered, a manuscript of Ghare Baire nearby

dialogue.text: As fame grows, he writes against aggressive nationalism, warning in essays and in Ghare Baire of the dangers when love of country hardens into worship of the collective self.

panels.shot: somber medium shot of Tagore reading a report of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, light falling starkly on the page

dialogue.text: In 1919, news from Amritsar reaches him: unarmed men, women and children fired upon in Jallianwala Bagh. His protest must now speak not in verse, but in a public act.

panels.shot: close-up of Tagore’s hand writing the letter returning his knighthood, the discarded knighthood insignia lying to one side

dialogue.text: He writes to the Viceroy, giving up the title of ‘Sir’, declaring he cannot accept honours from a government that has, in his words, stained its name with wanton cruelty.

panels.shot: medium shot of Tagore addressing a small gathering at Santiniketan after sending the letter, students and colleagues listening

dialogue.speaker: rabindranath_tagore
dialogue.text: An honour can be set aside; a conscience, once silenced, cannot be recovered.

panels.shot: gentle wide shot of Tagore walking with children at Santiniketan at dusk, Visva-Bharati buildings taking shape in the background

dialogue.text: Through awards, protests, praise and criticism, he returns to the same work: weaving song, school and world together, so that learning in this corner of Bengal may belong to all humankind.

panels.shot: final contemplative close-up of Tagore under a tree, eyes half-closed, children playing in the distance, faint outlines of distant cities in the sky

dialogue.text: Rooted in Bengali song yet heard in many tongues, his Gitanjali and Visva-Bharati ask still: can a voice stay true to its own soil and yet offer its song freely to the world?
